who: Follower of Jesus in the Gospels
why: Painters showed her weeping, and her name — pronounced maudlin in English — became the word for tearful sentimentality.
mean: Tearfully and excessively sentimental
story: Medieval English pronounced Magdalene as maudlin, which is why two Oxford and Cambridge colleges spelled Magdalen are still said that way. Centuries of paintings of her in tears did the rest.

why: Hymns of thanksgiving sung to him became the word for any song of praise.
mean: A song of praise or triumph
story: Paean was the doctor who patched the gods up when they were wounded in battle. The hymns sung to him in gratitude gave English the word for any outburst of praise.

why: His luxurious railway sleeping cars set the standard for comfortable long-distance travel.
mean: A luxurious railway carriage
story: Pullman built a whole company town for his workers, then cut wages without cutting rents. The strike that followed in 1894 shut down railways nationwide. He was buried under concrete to stop anyone digging him up.

why: He patented a light two-wheeled cab with the driver seated behind and above the passengers.
mean: A two-wheeled horse-drawn cab
story: Hansom was an architect who designed a cab as a sideline, sold the patent for £10,000 and was never paid. The cab made London's streets fast; he went back to designing churches.

why: He commissioned a small enclosed carriage that could turn in a narrow street.
mean: A small enclosed carriage
story: Brougham was a lawyer, a Lord Chancellor and a campaigner against slavery, and he is remembered for a carriage. He also popularised Cannes as a resort, more or less by accident, after being stranded there.

why: A four-wheeled carriage with a folding two-part roof was first built there.
mean: A carriage with a folding hood
story: The landau's roof splits in the middle and folds both ways, so passengers could be seen in fine weather and covered in bad. British royal processions still use them for exactly that reason.

who: Son of the sun god in Greek myth
why: He begged to drive the sun chariot, lost control, and scorched the earth.
mean: A light open carriage; a reckless driver
story: Phaethon took the reins of the sun for one day and nearly destroyed the world before Zeus shot him down. Naming a fast, unstable, open carriage after him was a joke that everyone at the time understood.

why: Edward VII took to wearing the local stiff felt hat and made it fashionable in Britain.
mean: A stiff felt hat with a curled brim
story: The future Edward VII visited the spa, liked the hat, and brought it home. Churchill wore one, and so did nearly every diplomat photographed between the wars.

who: Title character of George du Maurier's 1894 novel
why: The hat worn in the London stage version took the character's name.
mean: A soft felt hat with an indented crown
story: The novel that gave us the word Svengali also gave us the trilby — named not for the villain but for the heroine, from the hat worn onstage in the first London production.

why: They built a hard domed hat to protect gamekeepers' heads from low branches.
mean: A hard felt hat with a rounded crown
story: It was commissioned to stop gamekeepers being knocked off their horses by branches. The customer tested the prototype by putting it on the floor and stamping on it. It held, and he paid twelve shillings.

why: He knocked a tension spring off a shelf and watched it walk itself down.
mean: A coiled spring toy that walks downstairs
story: James was designing springs to steady instruments on rough seas when he knocked one off a shelf and watched it step end over end to the floor. His wife found the word slinky in a dictionary.

why: He built the cube to teach students about three-dimensional movement.
mean: A twisting cube puzzle
story: Rubik built it as a teaching aid and only realised he had made a puzzle when he scrambled it and could not put it back. It took him a month to solve his own invention.

why: The founder built the company name from the two Danish words.
mean: Interlocking plastic building bricks
story: Lego is short for leg godt, Danish for play well. By coincidence it also means I put together in Latin, which the company only discovered later and has been enjoying ever since.

why: The chef Escoffier created a peach dessert and a thin dry toast in her honour.
mean: Of dishes named for the singer: peach Melba, Melba toast
story: Escoffier served peach Melba in a swan carved from ice. The toast came later, when the singer was ill and could only manage something very thin and very dry. She got a dessert and a diet food.

why: He ordered the combination as a hangover cure at the Waldorf in 1894 and the chef put it on the menu.
mean: Poached eggs and ham on muffin with hollandaise
story: Benedict wandered into the Waldorf with a hangover and asked for buttered toast, bacon, poached eggs and hollandaise. The maitre d' was impressed enough to add it to the menu, swapping in muffin and ham.

why: A Venice barman named his peach-and-prosecco drink after a shade of pink in one of the painter's works.
mean: A cocktail of peach purée and prosecco
story: Giuseppe Cipriani mixed white peach purée with prosecco at Harry's Bar and thought the colour matched a saint's toga in a Bellini painting. A fifteenth-century artist therefore named a twentieth-century drink.

why: He asked a Florence barman to strengthen his Americano by replacing the soda with gin.
mean: A cocktail of gin, vermouth and Campari
story: The count had reportedly spent time in America as a rodeo rider and came back wanting something stronger than the drink named after his adopted country. The barman swapped soda for gin, and added an orange slice to mark the difference.

why: A British biscuit maker named a currant-filled biscuit after him following his 1854 visit.
mean: A biscuit with a layer of currants
story: Garibaldi unified Italy and was mobbed by crowds on a visit to England. Britain honoured the liberator of a nation by naming a flat currant biscuit after him, universally known in playgrounds as squashed-fly.

why: His cook coated almonds in caramelised sugar and named the sweet for his employer.
mean: A sweet of nuts in caramelised sugar
story: The cook is said to have got the idea from watching a kitchen boy eat spilled caramel and almonds. He named it for the marshal, opened a shop in Montargis, and that shop is still trading.

why: His chef is credited with the thick centre-cut steak served with a reduction sauce.
mean: A thick cut of beef tenderloin
story: Chateaubriand was a novelist, ambassador and foreign minister, and is now mostly a steak. His cook grilled the fillet between two lesser cuts so the outer meat burned and the middle stayed perfect, then threw the outer pieces away.

why: The cheese-enriched white sauce is traditionally credited to him or to his household.
mean: A béchamel sauce enriched with cheese
story: Mornay was a Huguenot leader nicknamed the Pope of the Protestants, who spent his life on theological argument. The attribution of the sauce is shaky, which puts it in good company among French sauces.

why: A city ordinance of 1390 set standards for its mustard, and the recipe using verjuice was developed there.
mean: A smooth sharp mustard
story: Dijon mustard is a recipe, not a place of origin — the name is not protected, so most of it is made elsewhere. The seeds mostly come from Canada, which would surprise a fourteenth-century Burgundian.

why: The hard alpine cheese has been made in the district since at least the twelfth century.
mean: A firm Swiss cheese
story: Gruyere famously has no holes, despite being the cheese most cartoons draw with them. The holes belong to Emmental, which comes from a different Swiss valley entirely.

who: Valley of the river Emme in Switzerland
why: The cheese with large holes was made in the valley's dairies.
mean: A Swiss cheese with large holes
story: The holes are bubbles of carbon dioxide from bacteria, and dairies can control their size by adjusting the temperature. For years the holes got smaller because the milk got cleaner — fewer hay particles for bubbles to form around.

why: The soft white-rinded cheese has been made in the region since at least the eighth century.
mean: A soft cheese with a white rind
story: At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, with Europe being carved up, the delegates held a competition to name the finest cheese. Brie won, and was dubbed the king of cheeses — the only crown that congress awarded.

why: The blue cheese was traditionally made and aged in the town.
mean: An Italian blue cheese
story: Legend says a distracted cheesemaker left curd overnight to chase a girl, added fresh curd in the morning to hide the lapse, and invented a blue cheese. Every blue cheese has a version of this story.

why: Any Italian cheese made from sheep's milk carries the name.
mean: An Italian sheep's-milk cheese
story: Not a place or a person — pecorino just means sheepish, in the literal sense. Roman legionaries were issued a daily ration of it, which makes it one of the oldest recorded packed lunches.

why: The cheese is made by cutting the stretched curd into pieces by hand.
mean: A soft fresh Italian cheese
story: Mozzarella is named after the action that makes it: the curd is heated, stretched like dough, and pinched off in lumps. The name means the cutting-off, which is exactly what the cheesemaker's hands are doing.

why: The new republic named itself after the man who led its liberation from Spain.
mean: Country in South America
story: Bolivia is one of very few countries named after a real person. Bolivar liberated six nations and died poor and disillusioned, writing that he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.

why: The republic took a Latinised form of his name at independence.
mean: Country in South America
story: Columbus never set foot in Colombia. The name was chosen by a revolutionary who wanted a title for the whole of Spanish America, and it ended up attached to one country.

why: A Spanish explorer named the islands after the then crown prince.
mean: Country in Southeast Asia
story: Named in 1543 for a Spanish prince who never visited. There have been serious proposals to change it since independence, on the grounds that the country is named after a foreign monarch who colonised it.

why: He was the first European to reach the island, and it was renamed in his honour in 1856.
mean: Island state of Australia
story: Tasman called it Van Diemen's Land after his sponsor. The name was changed in 1856 partly to shake off its association with convict transportation — so the island is named after the navigator instead of the governor.

why: The islands were claimed for France and named after the minister of the day.
mean: Island nation in the Indian Ocean
story: A hundred and fifteen islands in the Indian Ocean are named after a French finance minister who never saw them. He was in office for two years and is remembered nowhere else.

why: A German mapmaker labelled the new continent with the Latin form of his first name.
mean: The Americas
story: Martin Waldseemuller printed the name on a map in 1507 because Vespucci had argued it was a new continent rather than Asia. He later changed his mind and removed it — but a thousand copies were already out.

why: Romans named the islands for their large dogs; the bird was named after the islands.
mean: A small yellow songbird
story: The bird is named after the islands, and the islands are named after dogs — canis in Latin. So a small yellow songbird is, at two removes, named after a pack of large dogs.

why: English confused the American bird with a guinea fowl imported through Turkish merchants.
mean: A large game bird
story: The bird is American and the name is a mistake. English traders met a similar African bird sold by Turkish merchants and called it turkey; when the American bird arrived it inherited the wrong name. The Turkish for it is hindi, meaning Indian.

why: His notation and results run through almost every branch of mathematics.
mean: Relating to Euler's mathematics
story: Euler gave us the symbols e, i, f(x) and the sigma for sums. He also wrote the equation many mathematicians call the most beautiful there is, tying together five fundamental constants in seven characters.

why: He studied processes where the next step depends only on the current state, not the history.
mean: Of a process with no memory of its past
story: Markov developed his chains partly to win an argument, analysing the vowels and consonants in a Pushkin poem to prove a rival wrong about probability. The maths now runs speech recognition and page ranking.

why: He coined the word fractal and found the set that carries his name.
mean: Of fractal geometry
story: Mandelbrot asked how long the coast of Britain is, and answered: it depends on the length of your ruler. Measure in smaller steps and it gets longer without limit. That question opened up fractal geometry.

why: His reformulation of mechanics underpins quantum theory.
mean: Of Hamilton's formulation of mechanics
story: Hamilton solved a problem he had wrestled with for years while walking along a Dublin canal, and carved the formula into the stone of Broom Bridge with a penknife. A plaque marks the spot; mathematicians still visit.

why: Groups where order does not matter are named in his honour.
mean: Of a group where the order of operations does not matter
story: Abel proved that no formula can solve every fifth-degree equation, settling a question three centuries old. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-six, two days before a letter arrived offering him a professorship.

why: The unit measures the biological effect of radiation, not merely the energy absorbed.
mean: The SI unit of radiation dose equivalent
story: A gray measures energy absorbed; a sievert measures how much harm it does, which depends on the kind of radiation. The difference matters: the same energy from alpha particles is twenty times more damaging.

why: He noticed a compass needle twitch near a current-carrying wire, linking electricity and magnetism.
mean: A unit of magnetic field strength
story: Orsted spotted it during a lecture, in front of students, when a compass on the bench moved as he switched on a current. He said nothing at the time and spent three months checking before publishing.

why: He invented the barometer and proved that air has weight.
mean: A unit of pressure, one millimetre of mercury
story: Torricelli filled a tube with mercury, upended it in a dish, and found the column always fell to about the same height — leaving a vacuum above it. Philosophers had insisted for two thousand years that a vacuum was impossible.

who: Disputed — probably a rowdy London family of Irish origin in the 1890s
why: Police reports and music-hall songs of the period attached the name to street disorder.
mean: A violent troublemaker
story: The word appears suddenly in London newspapers in the summer of 1898, already meaning street rowdy. Whether the Houlihans were a real family, a music-hall joke, or both, nobody has ever settled.

why: Textile workers destroying machinery in 1811 signed their threats as followers of General Ludd.
mean: Someone opposed to new technology
story: The Luddites were not against machines in principle — they were skilled workers whose trade was being destroyed and who had no vote to object with. Ned Ludd, in whose name they wrote, probably never existed.

why: He designed a shell packed with musket balls that burst in the air over enemy troops.
mean: Fragments scattered by an exploding shell
story: Shrapnel spent his own money developing the shell over years before the army adopted it in 1803. He received a pension and a word in every language on earth. It is not a legacy most people would choose.

who: German nobleman (1720-1797) whose tall tales were published as fiction
why: The real baron's exaggerated stories inspired a book of impossible adventures.
mean: Of wildly exaggerated tales; a disorder involving feigned illness
story: The real baron told entertaining war stories. A writer published a wildly embroidered version without asking, making him a laughing stock across Europe — he spent his last years trying to sue, and hated the book.

why: The drink is generally held to be named for the queen whose reign saw Protestant executions.
mean: A cocktail of vodka and tomato juice
story: The naming is disputed — rival theories point to a Chicago bar and a Hollywood actress. The queen's own nickname is not disputed: roughly 280 people were burned during her five-year reign.

who: Village and beach in eastern Cuba
why: An American engineer working at the nearby iron mines mixed rum, lime and sugar and named it for the place.
mean: A rum, lime and sugar cocktail
story: Jennings Cox ran out of gin while entertaining guests near the Daiquiri mines and improvised with local rum. Hemingway later drank them in Havana by the dozen, and had a variant named after him in turn.

who: Island borough of New York City
why: The cocktail is credited to a Manhattan club in the 1870s.
mean: A cocktail of whiskey and vermouth
story: The island's own name comes from a Lenape word usually translated as place where we get bows, after the wood that grew there. So the drink is named after an island named after a bow-making forest.

who: Spanish for 'daisy' — and a common given name
why: Several women named Margarita are claimed as the origin; the drink is also a member of the daisy family of cocktails.
mean: A tequila, lime and orange-liqueur cocktail
story: At least six people have claimed to have invented it for a woman named Margarita. The likelier answer is dull: daisy was already a category of cocktail, and margarita is simply the Spanish for daisy.

who: English surveyor who patented tarmacadam in 1902
why: He saw a barrel of tar spilled on a road, covered with slag, and set hard — and patented the process.
mean: A tar-bound road surface
story: Hooley noticed a stretch of road outside an ironworks that was smooth and dustless, and learned a tar barrel had burst there and been covered with slag. He patented the accident and named it after McAdam.

why: Frederick Walton made the floor covering from oxidised linseed oil, and built the name from Latin.
mean: A hard-wearing floor covering
story: Walton got the idea from the rubbery skin that forms on a tin of old paint. He never trademarked the name, and a court ruled in 1878 that it had already become generic — the first product ever to lose a name that way.

why: He forced through a law requiring a load line on ships' hulls to stop dangerous overloading.
mean: A ship's load line; a rubber-soled canvas shoe
story: Plimsoll campaigned against coffin ships — overloaded and over-insured vessels worth more sunk than afloat. The shoe is named after the line too: the rubber band round the sole looks just like a ship's load mark.

why: He performed in a knitted one-piece that let audiences see the body at work.
mean: A close-fitting one-piece garment
story: Leotard invented the flying trapeze, practising over his father's swimming pool. He also inspired the song about the daring young man on the flying trapeze, and died of an infection at thirty-two.

why: He developed the oral polio vaccine given on a sugar cube.
mean: The oral polio vaccine
story: Sabin's vaccine could be swallowed rather than injected, which made mass campaigns possible in places with few doctors. Like Salk, he refused to patent it. The two men disliked each other for decades.

why: Hostages in a 1973 bank siege there defended their captors afterwards.
mean: Hostages developing sympathy for their captors
story: After six days in a bank vault, the hostages refused to testify against the robbers and some raised money for their defence. The psychiatrist who coined the term was himself part of the police negotiation.

why: His firm made the theatre organs and jukeboxes that carried the name into everyday speech.
mean: A theatre organ or jukebox
story: Wurlitzer organs were built to replace whole orchestras in silent-film theatres — one player, hundreds of pipes, plus drums, cymbals, birdsong and a car horn. Sound film arrived and the market vanished almost overnight.

why: He carved mandolin and guitar tops like violin tops, and the company kept his name.
mean: A make of guitar
story: Gibson had no formal training and carved instrument tops from a single piece of wood, arched like a violin, when everyone else bent flat sheets. He sold the patent and the company outgrew him entirely.

why: He designed the first mass-produced solid-body electric guitar and bass.
mean: A make of electric guitar
story: Fender never learned to play the guitar. He was a radio repairman who approached the instrument as an engineering problem — bolt the neck on so it can be replaced, and the whole thing can be built on a production line.

why: He developed the first effective polio vaccine and refused to patent it.
mean: The injected polio vaccine
story: Asked who owned the patent, Salk said the people did — could you patent the sun? United States polio cases fell from around 58,000 a year to almost none.

why: He was rarely filmed without a cigarette, and the slang came from his habit of letting it hang from his lip.
mean: To keep something to oneself instead of sharing
story: To bogart something is to hog it, from the way Bogart kept a cigarette clamped in his mouth without ever seeming to smoke it. The word entered wide use through a 1968 song.

why: He and his son collected plants worldwide for English gardens.
mean: A trailing houseplant with striped leaves
story: The Tradescants kept a museum of curiosities in Lambeth called the Ark, open to anyone who paid sixpence — the first public museum in England. Its collection became the founding core of Oxford's Ashmolean.

why: Linnaeus named the genus after his patron and predecessor at Uppsala.
mean: A yellow daisy-like flower, the black-eyed Susan
story: Rudbeck discovered the lymphatic system as a student, and later spent decades trying to prove that Sweden was the lost Atlantis. Linnaeus named the flower for him regardless.

why: Two botanists found the tree in Georgia and named it for their friend.
mean: A flowering tree, extinct in the wild
story: The Bartrams found this tree growing in one small patch in Georgia in 1765 and collected seeds. It has not been seen in the wild since 1803. Every franklinia alive today descends from those seeds.

why: The genus was named for the head gardener of the Vienna palace gardens.
mean: A large-leaved houseplant
story: Its other name is dumb cane: the sap contains needle-shaped crystals that make the mouth and throat swell, temporarily robbing anyone who chews it of speech. It remains a popular office plant.

why: The genus was named for the emperor's physician, who was also a botanist.
mean: A shade plant grown for its leaves
story: Hostas are grown for foliage rather than flowers, thrive in shade, and are eaten enthusiastically by slugs. Host himself was physician to the Austrian emperor and ran the imperial botanical garden.

who: English word meaning to scratch or grope about
why: The inventor renamed his word game, which had failed under two earlier names.
mean: A word-building board game
story: Alfred Butts, an out-of-work architect, counted letter frequencies on the front page of the New York Times to set the tile values. The game failed twice under other names before Scrabble stuck.

why: The inventor grew up in Ghana and took the name from Swahili.
mean: A tower-stacking block game
story: Leslie Scott's family played it with wooden blocks from a sawmill in Ghana. She named it from the Swahili kujenga, to build — which is slightly ironic for a game everyone plays in order to watch it fall over.

who: Economic term for exclusive control of a market
why: The game was adapted from The Landlord's Game, designed to demonstrate the harm monopolies cause.
mean: A property trading board game
story: Elizabeth Magie invented the original in 1904 as a protest against landlords hoarding property. Decades later a man sold a version to Parker Brothers as his own invention. She was paid five hundred dollars.

why: He composed the marches that defined American band music and asked for a tuba to be redesigned for marching.
mean: Of Sousa's marches; the sousaphone
story: Sousa wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever, the official national march of the United States. He also campaigned against recorded music, warning it would stop people learning instruments — a prediction with some merit.

why: His Alessandria workshop became the most famous felt hat maker in the world.
mean: A high-quality soft felt hat
story: A Borsalino takes around seven weeks and dozens of separate operations to make, mostly from rabbit felt. The firm was still going after more than 160 years, which very few hat companies can say.

why: An American doctor named his antiseptic after the pioneer of antiseptic surgery.
mean: An antiseptic mouthwash
story: Listerine was sold first as a surgical antiseptic, then as a floor cleaner and a cure for gonorrhoea. It only became a mouthwash when the makers popularised the word halitosis to convince people they had a problem.

why: He invented dynamite and left his fortune to fund prizes for benefit to humanity.
mean: The international prizes funded by Nobel's estate
story: A French paper mistakenly printed Nobel's obituary while he was alive, headlined The Merchant of Death Is Dead. He read his own reputation, disliked it, and rewrote his will to fund the prizes.

why: His novel described a man who found pleasure in being dominated.
mean: Taking pleasure in one's own suffering
story: Sacher-Masoch was a respected historian and novelist who deeply resented having his name turned into a clinical term. The psychiatrist Krafft-Ebing coined it anyway, and paired it with sadism in the same book.

why: He wrote at length about cruelty and spent much of his life imprisoned.
mean: Taking pleasure in others' suffering
story: De Sade spent roughly thirty-two years locked up and wrote much of his work in prison, including one novel on a continuous roll of paper hidden inside his cell wall.

why: He was known for swapping the opening sounds of words.
mean: A slip in which the first sounds of words are swapped
story: Spooner supposedly toasted our queer old dean rather than our dear old queen. Most famous examples were invented by students; he only ever admitted to one genuine slip in his whole career.

why: He crossed several berries, then abandoned the vines when his farm failed.
mean: A large dark berry crossed from several species
story: Boysen gave up and left the vines to die. Walter Knott tracked down the last survivors on the abandoned farm, nursed them back, and named the berry after the man who had quit.

why: He invented a written syllabary for Cherokee, and the giant tree was named in his honour.
mean: A giant redwood tree of California
story: Sequoyah could not read any language when he began, and worked twelve years to build a writing system from nothing. Within a few years most of the Cherokee nation was literate. The largest trees on Earth carry his name.

who: Roman goddess of grain and harvest
why: Grain crops were her gift, and Romans called them cerealia — her things.
mean: A grain crop; breakfast food made from grain
story: Your breakfast is named after a Roman goddess. Ceres governed grain and the harvest, and four thousand years later her name is printed on a cardboard box.

who: Roman god of fire and the forge
why: Romans believed the smoking island of Vulcano was the chimney of his underground workshop.
mean: A mountain that erupts molten rock
story: There is a small Italian island called Vulcano, named for the god the Romans thought was hammering beneath it. Every volcano on Earth — and on Mars — is named after one god's forge.

who: Roman god of doorways and beginnings
why: He had two faces, one looking back and one forward, which suits the turn of the year.
mean: The first month of the year
story: Janus guarded doorways with a face on each side, so he could see where you had been and where you were going at once. That is exactly what people do on the first of January.

why: March opened the campaigning season, when armies could move again.
mean: The third month of the year
story: March was once the first month of the Roman year. That is also why September, October, November and December mean seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth — they were, before two months were added at the front.

who: Roman queen of the gods, protector of marriage
why: Her month was considered the luckiest time to marry.
mean: The sixth month of the year
story: Juno looked after marriage, so Romans thought June the luckiest month for a wedding. Two thousand years later June is still the most popular wedding month in much of the world, for a reason almost nobody remembers.

why: Thor's day replaced the Roman day of Jupiter, who was also a thunder god.
mean: The fifth day of the week
story: The Romans called it Jupiter's day; the Anglo-Saxons swapped in their own thunder god. In French it is still jeudi, from Jove — so the same day is named after two different thunder gods in two languages.

who: Roman god of agriculture and time
why: It is the only English weekday still named after a Roman god rather than a Norse one.
mean: The seventh day of the week
story: Saturday is the odd one out. The Anglo-Saxons swapped most Roman gods for their own — Mars for Tiw, Jupiter for Thor — but nobody found a match for Saturn, so he kept his day.

who: Anglo-Saxon name for Odin, chief Norse god
why: Woden's day replaced the Roman day of Mercury.
mean: The fourth day of the week
story: Wednesday is Woden's day, and the silent d is the fossil of the missing name. Odin gave an eye for wisdom and hung from a tree for nine nights to learn the runes — none of which survives in the spelling except that d.

why: His followers resisted new Renaissance learning, so reformers turned his name into an insult.
mean: A slow or stupid learner
story: Duns Scotus was one of the sharpest minds of the Middle Ages. When fashions changed his stubborn followers were mocked as Dunses — so one of the cleverest men of his age now means the opposite.

why: His side whiskers were called burnsides, and people later flipped the halves of the word.
mean: Strips of facial hair grown down the sides of the face
story: They were burnsides first, after the general who wore an enormous pair. English swapped the two halves and produced sideburns — which now sounds like it describes the sides, purely by accident.

why: The small orange was shipped to Europe and America through Tangier.
mean: A small loose-skinned orange
story: Tangerines are named for the port they shipped from, not where they grew — the fruit is originally Chinese. Same pattern as the Panama hat: the name records the harbour, not the home.

who: Plain in Greece, site of a battle in 490 BC
why: A runner is said to have carried news of the victory to Athens and died on arrival.
mean: A long-distance race of about 42 kilometres
story: The distance was fixed at the 1908 London Olympics so the race could start at Windsor Castle and finish at the royal box — which is why every marathon since has been an oddly specific 42.195 kilometres.

who: Greek hero whose sacred grove stood outside Athens
why: Plato taught in that grove, and his school took the name of the ground it stood on.
mean: A place of learning or a society of scholars
story: Plato's school met in an olive grove sacred to a half-forgotten hero named Akademos. It ran for nearly nine hundred years, and every academy and academic traces back to that one patch of ground.

why: The unit of sound intensity was named the bel after him; a decibel is a tenth of one.
mean: A unit of loudness
story: The bel turned out to be too big for everyday use, so almost nobody uses it — we use tenths. Bell's mother and wife were both deaf, and his work on sound began as work on teaching deaf children to speak.

why: He sent specimens of the small fish to the British Museum, which named it after him.
mean: A small brightly coloured freshwater fish
story: The guppy had already been described and named twice before Guppy sent his specimens, so his name is not the official scientific one. It is the one everybody actually uses, which he would probably have settled for.

why: The small seedless citrus was found in his orphanage garden and named for him.
mean: A small sweet seedless citrus fruit
story: Brother Clement ran an orphanage outside Oran and noticed one tree producing unusually sweet, seedless fruit — a chance hybrid. Every clementine sold today descends from that single accidental tree.

why: The bacterium was isolated in his laboratory and named for him, though his assistant did the work.
mean: A bacterium causing food poisoning
story: Theobald Smith actually identified the organism. Salmon was his supervisor, and the naming followed the rank rather than the work — an old habit in science that has not entirely gone away.

why: Finns mocked his claim that Soviet bombs were food parcels, and named their petrol bombs a drink to go with the bread.
mean: A petrol bomb in a bottle
story: Molotov said Soviet aircraft were dropping food to starving Finns. The Finns called the cluster bombs Molotov bread baskets — and named their own petrol bombs Molotov cocktails, a drink to go with the meal.
